'''Bernhardt Patrick John O’Mara Bockris''' (5 January 1923 &ndash; 7 July 2013)<ref name="Fletcher"/> was a South African professor of chemistry, latterly at [[Texas A&M University]]. During his long and prolific career he published some 700 papers and two dozen books. His best known work is in [[electrochemistry]]{{sfn|Bockris, Devanathan, and Muller (1963)}}{{sfn|Bockris and Reddy (1970)}} but his output also extended to environmental chemistry, [[photoelectrochemistry]] and [[bioelectrochemistry]]. In the 1990s he experimented with [[cold fusion]] and transmutation, topics on which his unorthodox views provoked controversy.

== Early life ==

John Bockris was born on 5 January 1923, in [[Johannesburg, South Africa]]. His mother was Emmeline Mary MacNally and his father Alfred Bockris. He attended a sequence of schools in Brighton, including the preparatory school [[Withdean Hall]] from 1934 to 1937, and [[Xaverian College]], a Catholic [[secondary school]], from 1937 to 1940. His father was not present during his childhood: His mother and aunt earned their income from tailoring.<ref name="Fletcher">{{cite journal | last=Fletcher | first=Stephen | title=Obituary: Prof. John O'Mara Bockris (1923–2013) | journal=Journal of Solid State Electrochemistry | publisher=Springer Nature | volume=18 | issue=1 | date=1 December 2013 | issn=1432-8488 | doi=10.1007/s10008-013-2347-1 | pages=1–3| s2cid=98364240 | url=https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/2134/21091 }}</ref>

== University education ==

In 1940 Bockris began his scholarly education at Brighton Technical College which, in 1992, became the [[University of Brighton]]. Bockris wanted to study for a degree in Physics but this was not possible due to wartime staff shortages. Instead he took a two-year general degree in the natural sciences. In 1943, after a year of further study, he was accepted by [[Imperial College, London]] as a graduate student. He avoided conscription into the British armed forces due to his South African nationality.<ref name="Fletcher"/>

Bockris relates that his supervisor, [[Harold Ellingham]], provided minimal guidance and soon left the university altogether.<ref name="Life">{{cite journal | last=Bockris | first=John O’M. | title=An electrochemical life | journal=Journal of Solid State Electrochemistry | publisher=Springer Nature | volume=15 | issue=7–8 | date=1 January 2011 | issn=1432-8488 | doi=10.1007/s10008-011-1298-7 | pages=1763–1775| s2cid=195316792 }}</ref> Despite these obstacles, Bockris finished the research for his thesis, ''Electrochemistry of Non-aqueous Solutions,'' in two years, and received his doctorate in September 1945.<ref>Electrochemistry in Non-aqueous Solutions, J.O’M. Bockris, Thesis, Imperial College, 1945.</ref>

== Academic career ==
<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Bockris' Large Research Group University of Pennsylvania, 1965.png|thumb|right|Research group at University of Pennsylvania, 1965]] -->
<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Bockris' Third Research Group, Flinders University, Adelaide, Australia, 1975.png|The third research group, Flinders University, Adelaide, 1975|thumb|right]] -->
<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Bockris' Group 4 Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas 1985.png|Fourth research group Texas A&M University, 1985|thumb|right]] -->
Upon completion of his doctorate, at the age of 22, Bockris was immediately appointed to the faculty of Imperial College on the recommendation of [[Harry Julius Emeléus|Harry Emeléus]]. Over the course of the next eight years he supervised 28 graduate students with whom he co-authored a sufficient number of publications to qualify for his D.Sc., which he obtained in 1952. Among these students was [[Roger Parsons]], a future fellow of the [[Royal Society]], whom Bockris held in high regard.<ref name="Life"/>

Bockris moved to USA in 1953 to join the [[University of Pennsylvania]] as Professor of Chemistry, where he built a large and active research group. It was here that he published his best known work: the first model of the electrode-electrolyte surface to include the dipole moment of the solvent,{{sfn|Bockris, Devanathan, and Muller (1963)}} and his two-volume textbook ''Modern Electrochemistry.''{{sfn|Bockris and Reddy (1970)}} After 18 years in [[Philadelphia]], however, departmental politics became such that Bockris felt the need to move.<ref name="Fletcher"/><ref name="Life"/> During next appointment, at [[Flinders University]] of South Australia from 1971 onwards, his interests broadened to include [[photoelectrochemistry]] and environmental chemistry. In 1979 Bockris made his final move to [[Texas A&M University]] where he remained until his retirement in 1997. In his later years his research focus veered further toward sources of energy and he embraced positions on some controversial topics that acquired a certain celebrity but damaged his professional reputation.<ref name="Fletcher"/>

Electrode kinetics remained a major component of his research program throughout. Bockris also conducted investigations of high temperature chemistry, the determinants of electrolyte solubility, and [[Hydrogen embrittlement|hydrogen/metal interactions]].

Bockris was a prolific scholar, collaborator, and mentor. By the end of his career, he had authored, coauthored or edited more than 700 papers and two dozen books, and 85 students had obtained a PhD degree with his supervision.

==Controversies==

=== Hydrogen as a fuel ===
{{main|Photocatalytic water splitting}}
In 1970, Bockris, then a professor at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], said he had found a method for using sunlight to free hydrogen from water and coined the term "[[hydrogen economy]]" to describe the application of the anticipated technology.<ref name="timeline">{{cite web| url=http://www.hydrogenassociation.org/general/factSheet_history.pdf| title=The History of Hydrogen| author1=National Hydrogen Association| author2=United States Department of Energy| work=hydrogenassociation.org| publisher=National Hydrogen Association| page=1| access-date=17 December 2010| 
url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100714141058/http://www.hydrogenassociation.org/general/factSheet_history.pdf| archive-date=14 July 2010}}</ref> In 1975 he published a book on the subject.<ref name="Bockris 1975">{{cite book | author=Bockris | title=Energy, the solar hydrogen alternative | publisher=Wiley | location=New York | year=1975 | isbn=978-0-470-08429-8 | oclc=1502557 }}</ref> In 1982, at Texas A&M, he announced a "quantum leap" in his hydrogen-fuel technology through a "secret catalyst" that split water into hydrogen and oxygen even without the energy of sunlight. In 1984, he said he had found a material that facilitated complete conversion of sunlight to electricity. All of these "discoveries" were eventually attributed to basic errors in his research, although Bockris himself never acknowledged his mistakes.<ref name=HP>Brian Wallstin, [http://houstonpress.com/1994-04-07/news/aggie-alchemy/1 "Aggie Alchemy: John Bockris was known around Texas A&M as a chemist interested in "weird science." Joe Champion gave him all he could handle."], ''Houston Press'', 7 April 1994</ref>
<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Bockris' lab boris cahan helps FCS Saluga determine vibration potentials.png|thumb|right|Boris Cahan helps FCS Saluga determine vibration potentials]]  -->

=== Cold fusion ===
{{main|Cold fusion}}
Bockris performed a series of cold fusion experiments in the wake of the announcement in 1989 by [[Stanley Pons|Pons]] and [[Martin Fleischmann|Fleischmann]] that their electrolysis of [[heavy water]] had produced results consistent with [[nuclear fusion]].<ref name="CF">{{cite journal | last1=Fleischmann | first1=Martin | last2=Pons | first2=Stanley | title=Electrochemically induced nuclear fusion of deuterium | journal=Journal of Electroanalytical Chemistry and Interfacial Electrochemistry | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=261 | issue=2 | year=1989 | issn=0022-0728 | doi=10.1016/0022-0728(89)80006-3 | pages=301–308}}</ref> Many groups attempted similar experiments: Bockris' research group was one of few to provide results that supported those of Pons and Fleischmann, reporting decisive evidence of tritium production.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Packham | first1=N.J.C. | last2=Wolf | first2=K.L. | last3=Wass | first3=J.C. | last4=Kainthla | first4=R.C. | last5=Bockris | first5=J.O'M. | title=Production of tritium from D2O electrolysis at a palladium cathode | journal=Journal of Electroanalytical Chemistry and Interfacial Electrochemistry | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=270 | issue=1–2 | year=1989 | issn=0022-0728 | doi=10.1016/0022-0728(89)85059-4 | pages=451–458}}</ref> Their results were greeted with widespread skepticism. [[Gary Taubes]] wrote an editorial in [[Science (magazine)|Science]] suggesting that their cells might have been spiked with [[tritiated water]].<ref>{{citation|last=Taubes|first=Gary |title=Cold fusion conundrum at Texas A&M |journal=Science|volume=248|issue=15 June 1990| pages=464–5| year=1990| doi=10.1126/science.248.4961.1299| bibcode=1990Sci...248.1299T| pmid=17735269}}</ref> An academic tribunal at Texas A&M eventually ruled out fraud, declaring that intentionally spiked experiments gave different results.<ref>{{cite news| title=Texas Panel Finds No Fraud in Cold Fusion Experiments| work=[[The New York Times]]| first1=John| last1=Poston| first2=Edward S.| last2=Fry| first3=Joseph B.| last3=Natowitz| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/11/20/science/texas-panel-finds-no-fraud-in-cold-fusion-experiments.html| access-date = 24 September 2009| date=20 November 1990}}</ref> Bockris, seemingly inured to criticism,<ref name="Fletcher"/> published his side of the controversy in a stubborn defense of academic freedom.<ref name="Accountability">{{cite journal | last=Bockris | first=J. O'M. | title=Accountability and academic freedom: The battle concerning research on cold fusion at Texas A&M university | journal=Accountability in Research | publisher=Informa UK Limited | volume=8 | issue=1–2 | year=2000 | issn=0898-9621 | doi=10.1080/08989620008573968 | pages=103–119| s2cid=142082522 }}</ref>

Though his professional reputation declined after this episode, the [[International Conference on Cold Fusion|International Society for Condensed Matter Nuclear Reactions]] continued to hold Bockris in high esteem, awarding him its Preparata Medal in 2012.<ref name="International Society for Condensed Matter Nuclear Science – ISCMNS.org 2009">{{cite web | title=ISCMNS Prizes | website=International Society for Condensed Matter Nuclear Science – ISCMNS.org | date=8 October 2009 | url=http://www.iscmns.org/prizes.htm | access-date=27 August 2018 | archive-date=11 April 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150411034508/http://www.iscmns.org/prizes.htm | url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Transmutation ===
In 1993, Bockris claimed to be experimenting with the transmutation of elements, specifically of base metals into [[gold]]. The scientist received a degree of media attention for these extraordinary claims, to the extent that other academics at Texas A&M felt that the institution's reputation was suffering from the connection to the discredited "science" of [[alchemy]]. An editorial by Mike Epstein in the ''[[Journal of Scientific Exploration]]'' describes what happened next:

:A petition signed by 23 of the 28 distinguished professors at Texas A&M called on the university provost to strip Bockris of his title as distinguished professor. The petition follows a letter written by 11 full professors in the chemistry department (out of the department's 38 full professors) calling on Bockris to resign and remove the "shadow" he has cast over the department. The petition from the distinguished professors said "For a trained scientist to claim, or support anyone else's claim to have transmuted elements is difficult for us to believe and is no more acceptable than to claim to have invented a gravity shield, revived the dead or to be mining green cheese on the moon. We believe that Bockris' recent activities have made the terms 'Texas A&M' and '[[Texas A&M Aggies|Aggie]]' objects of derisive laughter throughout the world..."<ref name="mikeepstein.com">{{cite web | title=Academic Freedom or Scientific Misconduct? | website=mikeepstein.com | date=29 April 2012 | url=http://www.mikeepstein.com/path/free.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120429045551/http://www.mikeepstein.com/path/free.html | archive-date=29 April 2012 | url-status=unfit | access-date=27 August 2018}}</ref>

Epstein's conclusion, however, was a defense of academic freedom:<ref name="mikeepstein.com"/>

:"However, I would remind those who seek his ouster or demotion that their actions threaten the core of academic freedom. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary proof, but no one should be punished for attempting to provide that proof".

The petition failed, and Dr. Bockris was eventually absolved by a four-professor panel of violating Texas A&M standards in proposing, conducting or reporting controversial research.<ref>Report: Committee of inquiry. Re: Allegation of Scientific Misconduct against J. O'M Bockris, 31 January 1994. Texas A&M university, Office of the Vice President for Research and Associate Provost for Graduate Studies.</ref>

In [[List of Ig Nobel Prize winners#1997|1997]], Bockris was awarded an [[Ig Nobel Prize]] in the field of Physics for his work in cold fusion and transmutation.<ref name="Ignobel">{{cite web| last=Cromie| first=William J.| title=Ignominious Ig Nobels Ignite Hilarity at Harvard| website=news.harvard.edu| date=11 May 2016| url=http://news.harvard.edu/gazette/1997/10.16/IgnominiousIgNo.html| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160511050541/http://news.harvard.edu/gazette/1997/10.16/IgnominiousIgNo.html| archive-date=11 May 2016| url-status=dead| access-date=27 August 2018| quote=The Ig Nobel for Physics was inflicted on John Bockris of Texas A&M University for his work with cold fusion, the century's biggest nondiscovery. Bockris was also praised for his efforts to turn lead into gold.}}</ref> The awardee declined to accept the trophy in person.

== Honours and awards ==
* Médaille d’honneur, from the [[Catholic University of Leuven (1835–1968)|University of Louvain]] in Belgium, 1951.
* [[Breyer-Gutmann Medal]], [[Australian Chemical Society]], 1975.
* The Chemical Lecture Award, the [[Swedish Academy]], 1979.
* Membership of [[Swedish Academy of Engineers]] as foreign member, 1979.
* The [[Faraday Medal (electrochemistry)|Faraday Medal]] of the Electrochemistry Group of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]], 1981
* Award of the [[Chemical Society of the USA]] for Developments of Modern Fuels, 1982.
* Award in Teaching Electrochemistry, [[Electrochemical Society]], 1985.
* Honorary doctorate from the [[University of La Plata]], Argentina, 1986.
* Honorary PhD of the [[University of Hokkaido]], Japan, 1988.
* Member of the [[Serbian Academy of Sciences]], 1992.
* [[Volta Medal]] in Physics associated with the Bicentenary of Volta, Pavia, Italy, 2000.
* [[Ig Nobel Prize]] in Physics, [[List of Ig Nobel Prize winners#1997|1997]]
